en: I bow to him who taught the lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) of dependently arisen phenomena— he whose wisdom is peerless, inconceivable, and beyond demonstration. Just as you yourself [perceived] the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) in the Mahāyāna, [so have I].
In the same way, out of compassion, that which was known has been taught to the wise:
you have declared that what arises from conditions is unarisen;
because it is not born by way of intrinsic nature, it is revealed as empty.
Just as an echo arises here depending upon a sound,
so too does the arising of existence occur like a magical illusion, a mirage, or a city of the Gandharvas;
it is like a reflection, a magical illusion, a mirage, a city of the Gandharvas, or a reflected image.
If [things] were unarisen along with dreams, there would be no such thing as seeing them and so forth.
Just as these are known to be produced from causes and conditions and are thus considered created,
so too, O Lord, you have stated that the entire universe born of conditions is conventional.
All this that is produced is merely the prattle of fools;
it resembles an empty fist, revealed as something that does not correspond to reality. Since no produced thing has ever arisen, what then could be present?
Through the destruction of what would there be a past? What does that which desires to arise depend upon? (8) An entity is not born from itself, nor from another, nor from both;
it is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent. How, then, could there be the arising of anything? (9)
In that which is unborn, there is no intrinsic nature; how, then, could there be arising from itself?
Precisely because the absence of intrinsic nature is established, arising from another is also impossible.
If there were selfhood, there would be otherness; if there were otherness, selfhood is required.
The establishment of these two is said to be relative, like "this shore" and "the other shore.
When it does not depend on anything at all, how could anything then exist?
When it does not depend on "long," how could there then be "short" and so forth?
When existence exists, non-existence exists; likewise, when length exists, shortness exists.
When non-existence exists, existence exists; therefore, both are not real.
The same applies to unity and plurality, as well as the past, the future, and so forth.
How could defilement and purification, or the correct and the false, exist by themselves?
For when no entity exists at all by itself, what then exists?
That which is called "other" does not exist without its own intrinsic nature.
When there is neither intrinsic nature (svabhāva) nor extrinsic nature (parabhāva) of things,
then what dependent nature (paratantra) could there be for one seized by the obsession of grasping at things?
From the very beginning, they are born equal and are extinguished by their own nature.
Therefore, you have declared that all phenomena are unproduced in reality;
O wise one, you have revealed that form and the other aggregates are devoid of intrinsic nature,
being like foam, bubbles, illusions, clouds, mirages, and plantain trunks.

If that which is perceived by the sense faculties were to exist in its true nature, then fools would be knowers of reality; what then would be the use of the knowledge of reality? [They would be] insentience, lack of authority, or even the state of being indeterminate.
You have stated that there is a perverted understanding of the sense faculties;
thinking that the world does not proceed according to reality because it is shrouded by ignorance, you have declared this to be the case as it truly is.
"It exists" is the view of eternalism; "it does not exist" is the view of nihilism.
Therefore, this Dharma has been taught by you as free from these two extremes.
For that reason, all phenomena have been declared by you to be free from the four logical alternatives.
Even for consciousness, they are unknowable; how much less can they be the domain of words?
Just as the appearance of two moons produced by a dream or a magician’s trick is not a real thing, so too has the world been seen by you as neither real nor unreal.
Just as a son in a dream is born, remains, and perishes,
so too have you stated that the world, in its ultimate sense, is neither born, nor does it remain, nor does it perish.
Just as an occurrence from a cause is seen in a dream, so it is with anything else.
The arising of all phenomena is held to be just like their passing away.
Just as suffering born of passion and the like constitutes affliction and cyclic existence,
so too is liberation taught by you to be like a dream, resulting from the fulfillment of the accumulations.
"Born" is likewise "not born," and "come" is also "gone";
similarly, the one who knows is both "bound" and "liberated. One who knows reality does not desire this duality.
For that which has no origination at all, what cessation could there be?
Because it appears like an illusory elephant, its primordial peace is established by implication.
Just as an illusory elephant is considered produced yet not produced,
so too the entire universe is both produced and, in reality, unproduced.

By immeasurable Lords of the World, the nirvana of each of the immeasurable beings has been brought about; yet, in truth, not a single being has been liberated by them. Those beings who attain nirvana have clearly never been born.
"O Great Sage, it has been declared that no one has been liberated by anyone.
Just as a magical creation is devoid of substance, so too is everything else;
you have stated that the entire world is devoid of substance, and likewise the agent."
Even an agent, when produced by another, does not transcend the state of being produced;
or else, it follows that the agent would be the performer of its own action.
You have declared loudly that this entire world is a mere name.
The referent does not exist as something separate from the designation.
Therefore, all phenomena have been revealed as mere conceptual construction;
yet even that conceptual construction is said to be non-existent, by which emptiness is conceptually constructed.
That which transcends the duality of existence and non-existence, yet is not transcended by anything;
that which is neither knowledge nor the object of knowledge, neither existent nor non-existent;
that which is neither one nor many, neither both nor neither—[that is the ultimate reality].
Without abode, unmanifest, inconceivable, and invisible;
that which neither arises nor passes away, which is neither annihilated nor eternal—
that is like space, beyond the sphere of syllables and cognition.
That which is dependent origination is itself considered by you to be emptiness;
such is the True Dharma, and the Tathāgata is equal to it.
That reality is also held to be the ultimate truth, suchness, and the substantial entity.
That which is real is non-deceptive; because he has awakened to that, he is called "Buddha.
Therefore, in reality, there is no difference between the Buddhas and the realm of sentient beings.
By that [realization], they are considered to have attained the equality of self and others.
Emptiness is not other than things, nor do things exist without it;
therefore, you have revealed that dependently arisen things are empty.
Conventional reality arises from causes and conditions and is dependent upon others.
The dependent nature is thus proclaimed; however, the ultimate reality is unconditioned.
It is called intrinsic nature, primordial essence, reality, substance, entity, and existence.
Indeed, a constructed entity does not exist, yet the dependent nature is found to exist.
You have declared that the assertion "it exists" regarding an imagined entity is a superimposition (samāropa),
and that the assertion "it does not exist" reveals nihilism (uccheda) due to the annihilation of what was produced.
Through the knowledge of reality, neither annihilation nor permanence is accepted.
The entire world is considered empty of substantial reality, resembling a mirage. Just as the water of a mirage is neither annihilated nor eternal,
so too is the entire world said to be neither annihilated nor eternal.
For one for whom a substance arises, there would follow its annihilation and so forth;
for such a person, it follows that the world is either finite or infinite.
Just as the object of knowledge exists when there is knowledge, so too does knowledge exist when the object of knowledge exists.
"When both [subject and object] are unarisen, what then exists?
Having thus clearly explained this through analogies such as an illusion, the supreme physician taught the True Dharma, which is the remedy for all views.

This is that supreme reality, the teaching on the meaning of the absence of intrinsic nature; it is the unsurpassed medicine for those seized by the grasping at existence. O Dharmayājñika, by this very means, the unsurpassed Dharma-sacrifice is performed.
Constantly desired throughout the three worlds, doorless and unhindered,
you have let out this wondrous lion’s roar of selflessness, which cuts through the fear of grasping at real entities and strikes terror into the deer-like heretics. (NagAst 53–54)
The drum of the Dharma, profound with the teaching of emptiness, has been struck;
the conch of the Dharma, with its great sound of the absence of intrinsic nature, has been blown.
This nectar of the Buddhas' teaching is declared to be the dowry of the Dharma.

Indeed, it has been taught by you that the definitive meaning (nītārtha) is precisely the emptiness of all phenomena. But that teaching concerning arising and cessation, as well as sentient beings, living souls, and so forth— which was spoken by you, O Protector— is of interpretable meaning (neyārtha) and is merely conventional (saṃvṛti).

"He who has reached the absolute further shore of the ocean of the perfection of wisdom, he is rich in the jewels of meritorious qualities and has crossed to the other side of the ocean of your virtues.
Having thus praised the Lord of the World, who is inconceivable and beyond demonstration, [he said: NagAst_58.
By whatever merit has been acquired by me, may the world become equal to you.
Thus ends the *Acintyastava*.
